passages.happening:
Tyre had said of Jerusalem that the gate to the nations was broken and swung open to her: ‘now that she lies in ruins I will be filled’ (verse 2). So God says, ‘Behold, O Tyre, I am against you, and I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves’ (verse 3). They will tear down her walls and towers, and God will scrape her soil away ‘and make her a bare rock’ (verse 4), a place to spread nets in the sea (verse 5).

God will bring against Tyre ‘Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings’ (verse 7), with horses, chariots and troops, siege ramps and battering rams (verses 8-11). ‘They will plunder your wealth and pillage your merchandise’ and throw her stones and timber into the water (verse 12). ‘You will never be rebuilt’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Tyre was the leading city of Phoenicia, on the coast of what is now southern Lebanon. Its main city stood on a rocky island a short distance offshore, with settlements on the mainland. Its position made it almost impossible for land armies to take, and its fleets and colonies, Carthage among them, gave it trade across the Mediterranean. Hiram of Tyre had supplied David and Solomon with cedar.

Tyre's taunt is commercial. Judah sat astride inland trade routes, and with Jerusalem gone Tyre expected to take its share of the traffic. Its sin was to treat a neighbor's ruin as a business opportunity. The date in verse 1 gives the year but not the month; either way, it belongs to the time of Jerusalem's fall.
passages.later: Isaiah had said, ‘Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste’ (Isaiah 23:1). Amos condemned Tyre for handing over exiles and breaking ‘a covenant of brotherhood’ (Amos 1:9).
passages.hard:
Nebuchadnezzar did not destroy Tyre, and a city called Tyre still exists. Did this prophecy fail?

The difficulty is real and old. According to the historian Josephus, citing Phoenician records, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years, probably about 586 to 573 BC, and the siege ended with Tyre's submission, not its destruction. Tyre was later rebuilt and is a city today. Readers respond in several ways. Many point to verse 3, which speaks of many nations coming like waves, and to verse 12, which shifts from he to they; on this reading the prophecy describes a process that began with Nebuchadnezzar and was completed by later conquerors, notably Alexander the Great, who in 332 BC took the island city by building a causeway with rubble from the old mainland town. Some add that the ancient island city lies largely in ruins beneath the later town. Others read the language as the stylized speech of judgment oracles, which announce the end of a proud power in total terms; Tyre as an independent sea power did come to an end.

The book itself keeps the tension. In 29:17-20, about sixteen years later, Ezekiel records that Nebuchadnezzar got no wages from Tyre and promises him Egypt instead. Many readers find it significant that the book did not rewrite the earlier oracle.
passages.asks: Tyre saw its neighbor's ruin as its own gain. Ask where you are tempted to profit from someone else's loss. And ask what it would mean to grieve with them instead.

passages.t: The princes of the sea lament
passages.happening:
The coastlands will tremble at the sound of Tyre's fall (verse 15). The princes of the sea will step down from their thrones, take off their robes, sit on the ground and tremble (verse 16). They will lament: ‘How you have perished, O city of renown inhabited by seafaring men’ (verse 17).

God will bring the deep over Tyre and send her down to the Pit, to the people of long ago (verses 19-20). ‘I will make you an object of horror, and you will be no more. You will be sought, but will never be found’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The lament of the sea princes uses real mourning customs: stepping down from thrones, removing robes, sitting on the ground. The coastlands were the islands and coastal peoples of the Mediterranean who traded with Tyre and depended on it.

The Pit is a common Old Testament name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a place beneath the earth where the dead of all the ancient peoples lie. A city that ruled the sea will go down beneath it.
passages.later: Isaiah too pictured the merchants of the sea mourning Tyre (Isaiah 23:2-8). A psalm says God will bring men of bloodshed and deceit ‘down to the Pit of destruction’ (Psalm 55:23).
passages.asks: The whole sea trembled when Tyre fell. Ask what you rely on that seems too big to fall. And ask what it would mean to build your life on what cannot be shaken.
